lawyer:
B.K. Das, Advocate ----- for appellant 
A. Hasib with Mokhtar Hossain, Advocate ----- for respondent
parties:
Abdul Mujib Chowdhury
Vs.
Syed Abdul Mutalib & Others
full_judgment:
M. H. Rahman, J.:- This appeal is directed against the judgment of the court of appeal below decreeing the plaintiff's suit for partition in preliminary form. The plaintiffs' case is that they purchased /10/- annas share of the suit land on 25.5.1963 and the defendant purchased the remaining share subsequently on 7.6.63. Joint possession was given to the plaintiffs and the defendant. It was stipulated that the defendant would enjoy their share in the southern part and the plaintiff’s would enjoy their share in the southern portion. There was a misguiding stipulation in the purchase-document to the effect that plaintiffs would get 30 cubits from the north in their /10/- annas share and the defendant would get/6/- annas share in the north without specifying dimensions in cubits. This was done by the defendant on whom the plaintiffs relied for negotiation, execution and registration of the kabala. When the defendant demanded specific possession of his share in the northern side the plaintiffs could not agree to the demand as the southern side of the 1st schedule land was far less in area and dimension than the northern side. Thereafter the defendant brought Title Suit No. 339 of 1964 in the 1st Court of Sadar, Munsif, Sylhet. On transfer to the Additional Court of the Munsif the suit was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 74 of 1965. The defendant got an ex-parte decree for specific possession in accordance with the description given by him in that suit. There was a rehearing of the matter and the suit was restored to its original file and number. The plaintiffs had two tenants, Israil Ali and Syed Mahibul Islam, in their northern rooms. As plaintiff No. 1 was in Karachi his mother, plaintiff' No. 2, used to depend on Syed Mahibul Islam. Defendant No. 1 in collusion with Syed Mahibul Islam filed a solenama purported to have been executed by plaintiff No. 2 and by his two tenants though in fact neither plaintiff No. 2 nor Israel All executed the same. The plaintiffs further contended that they did not empower their lawyer to execute the Solenama. The Compromise decree was put to execution in Title Execution Case No. 7 of 1967 in the 1st Munsif Court, Sylhet. When the defendant was about take delivery of possession through a lawyer Commissioner plaintiff No. 2 brought Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 for a declaration that the alleged compromise decree was null and void, but the suit was dismissed on 31.8.67. Thereafter the defendant proceeded with the execution case and got delivery of possession on 8.9.67 in the northern portion of the suit premises in excess of his due share. Thereafter the plaintiffs demanded on 6.1.63 partition of the suit property by metes and bounds, but the defendant did not agree. 

 2. The defendant contested the suit denying the material allegations in the plaint. He contended that the suit was not maintainable and it was barred by estoppel, waiver acquiescence and under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also asserted the suit was hit by the final decision of Title Suit No. 74 of 1965 and Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 and that plaintiffs could not got any decree without setting aside the decree passed in the former title suit No. 74 of 1965 on the basis of which of the delivery of possession was obtained through court. Further case of the defendant is that the plaintiffs purchased specific land in the southern portion denoted by specific measurement, leaving out the land to the north, and as the plaintiffs purchased earlier the question of joint possession did not arise. Besides, Title Suit No. 314 of 1965 filed by the plaintiff was allowed to be dismissed for non-prosecution; and that the appeal against the decree of dismissal of Title Suit No. 122 of 1967 was also dismissed. 

 4. The court of appeal below reversed the decision of the trial court and decreed the suit in preliminary form. It found that the suit was not hit by res judicata as the question of partition was not a point at issue in Title Suit No 74 of 1965. It held that plaintiffs and the defendant intended to purchase /10/-annas and -6/- annas share and there was no evidence on record that there were actual measurements at the time of incorporating the stipulation as to measurement by cubits in the schedules to the respective kabalas. The court of appeal below found that the stipulations were incorporated in the documents for convenience of possession of the parties without intending any final partition. 

 7. In all the three cases there was a compromise between the parties to the suit and the decree was passed in terms of the com-promise and put to execution. 

 8. Title suit No. 74 of 1965 between the plaintiffs and the defendant and others were concluded by the compromise by which the parties admitted their respective title and agreed to demarcate their respective shares in the properties in question and the compromise was put to execution: In A.I.R. 1928, Lahore, 938, it was held that where in the execution of a decree possession was alleged to have been given in a property not covered by the decree the suit for recovery of the excess land was barred under section 47 of the Code, and the appropriate remedy to recover the ex-ecess property was by way of an application under section 47. In A. I. R. 1957 (Patna) 700, where the plaintiffs' property was wrongly sold in execution it was held that the suit for declaration of title and delivery of possession with regard to the land wrongly sold in execution was barred under section 47. In 26 D.L.R. 279, a contractual obligation created on the basis of a solenama was considered as a question of adjustment within the meaning of section 47 of the Code and a separate suit for specific performance of that obligation was held to be hit by section 47. In that case on the prayer of the plaintiff appellants the matter was remanded to the trial court and the plaint filed in the suit was directed to be treated as an application under section 47. 

 9. It appears that there was no clear evidence that plaintiffs and defendant were given distinct possession in the suit property by the vender. The descriptions as to the respective shares of the plaintiff and the defendant and as to measurement of the land caused misgivings in the minds of the parties. The series of litigations between the parties were ultimately concluded by the compromise decree. After execution of the compromise decree it is clear that the suit property ceased to be a partible property and the suit for partition was not available to the plaintiffs. Again as the defendants gave up Rs. 1000/- as consideration for the compromise the present suit which is in effect directed against that compromise must be held as hit by the principle of estoppel. 

 11. There is no doubt that the plaintiffs' grievance that the defendant get more land than his due share arose from the execution of the compromise decree and any prayer for correction or adjustment of the execution of the decree should determined by the executing court and not by way of a separate suit. Finding his difficulties Mr. Hasib the learned Advocate for the respondent has prayed that the plaint should be converted into an application under section 47 of the Code and be sent down for disposal by the executing court. The Court of the Munsif, Sadar, Sylhet was the executing court. The suit was, however, fined before the second court of the Subordinate Judge, Sylhet. Hence, the suit cannot be converted to an application under section 47 of the Code. In view of the above I allow the appeal. The judgment and decree of court of appeal below are hereby set aside and those of the trial court are affirmed.
